title: Exomiser prioritization contributed to rare-disease diagnoses in the 100,000 Genomes Project pilot
summary: Phenotype-driven ML prioritization helped diagnose 25% of 2,183 probands in the NHS pilot; a quarter of diagnoses were immediately actionable.
account: The 100,000 Genomes Project rare-disease diagnosis pilot appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine, 11 November 2021. It applied Exomiser's phenotype-based prioritization to genomes from 2,183 families in the English National Health Service (NHS). Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders. 92% of the 490 diagnoses came from applied gene panels or Exomiser's top five candidates. Clinicians reported 134 of 533 genetic diagnoses, 25%, were of immediate clinical actionability, including medication changes, surveillance recommendations, clinical trial eligibility and reproductive planning.
purpose: Score and rank candidate causative variants against patient phenotypes to make genome-scale rare-disease diagnosis tractable for clinical teams.
system: Exomiser phenotype-driven variant prioritization (machine-learning-assisted scoring and ranking)
developer: Not named in the cited sources; the pilot's phenotype-based prioritization analysis was led by Damian Smedley's team at Queen Mary University of London and Genomics England.
deployer: Genomics England and NHS Genomic Medicine Centers
segment: Families with undiagnosed rare disease in a national health system

ratings.reason: Clinicians reported that 134 of 533 genetic diagnoses (25%) were of immediate clinical actionability, including medication changes and surveillance. That is a cohort figure and no individually attributable changed outcome is cited.

Exomiser's top five candidates together with applied panels accounted for 92% of the 490 diagnoses. That is an aggregate reduction in manual interpretation burden across the pilot rather than a discrete organizational event.
A 25% diagnostic yield across 2,183 families is reported for a national health-system pilot rather than population-wide deployment.

ai_role.statement: Exomiser scored and ranked candidate variants against each proband's phenotype. The pilot reports that diagnoses were detected in 77% of top-ranked candidate variants and that panels and Exomiser's top five were complementary. Clinical confirmation and reporting were performed by NHS diagnostic laboratories and clinicians, not by the software. Neither cited source says who developed Exomiser. The pilot's prioritization analysis was led by Damian Smedley's team at Queen Mary University of London and Genomics England, who are among the paper's authors. An independent evaluation is cited alongside it.

evidence.quote: With the use of phenotype-based prioritization with the Exomiser to score and rank the most likely causative variants, diagnoses were detected in 77% of the top-ranked candidate variants.

headline: Exomiser helps diagnose 25% of 2,183 probands in the NHS pilot
metric: Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders

comparator.against: the virtual panel-based pipeline (applied gene panels) alone
comparator.before: A total of 322 (66%) of the 490 diagnoses that were based on SNVs or indels from the genomes were made with the virtual panel–based pipeline
comparator.after: diagnoses were detected in 77% of the top-ranked candidate variants, in 86% of the top three candidates, and in 88% of the top five candidates
comparator.quote: With the use of phenotype-based prioritization with the Exomiser to score and rank the most likely causative variants, diagnoses were detected in 77% of the top-ranked candidate variants, in 86% of the top three candidates, and in 88% of the top five candidates (Fig. 2D). Use of the Exomiser and applied panels was complementary — 92% of the 490 diagnoses were made with the applied panels or the Exomizer top five candidates (last blue bar in Fig. 2D).

Benefit type set to Improved Physical Health under Trustible's full taxonomy of 23 types; it was Improved Knowledge Discovery among the six first used.
